title: Memory Safety Bugs in Rust Standard Library
excerpt: Knowing What You Trust: Three patterns behind memory safety bugs we found in Rust's standard library, and why Rust's safety model still matters even though it isn't perfect.
content_html:
Microsoft’s FORGE Lab found several memory safety issues in Rust’s standard library (std and core), including cases where code written entirely in safe Rust can trigger undefined behavior. The research used Hyenas, FORGE’s frontier research version of codename MDASH, an AI-powered vulnerability-scanning system. The findings reveal three recurring patterns of misplaced trust in unsafe code: trusting code not to panic, trusting user-provided implementations to be correct, and trusting the underlying system.

Rust’s safety guarantees are precisely what make these findings interesting. Its rich type system and ownership model rule out whole classes of memory-safety issues, but much of the standard library relies on unsafe code underneath its safe APIs. When that code breaks its safety contract, even safe Rust can encounter behavior the language is designed to prevent.

Rust’s memory-safety guarantees are increasingly important as the language becomes part of software that billions of people rely on every day. Billions of people are estimated to interact with Rust-based software or operating systems daily, often without knowing it. Microsoft made Rust a Tier-1 internal language alongside C++, C#, and TypeScript, GitHub rewrote the Copilot agent runtime in Rust, and Bun, Android, the Linux kernel, and Cloudflare are moving code to it as well. Much of this software relies on Rust’s foundational libraries, core and std, and the safety guarantees of the APIs they provide. Bugs in those libraries can have consequences well beyond the code where they originate.

Unsafe Rust has been a long-running interest for us. Our team includes the people behind Rudra, a static analyzer that looked for memory-safety bugs across the Rust ecosystem in 2021. We also write many of our own tools in Rust, so its safety is more than a research topic for us. This year, we took a closer look at the standard library to see what kinds of mistakes still show up in its unsafe code today.

In this post, we share some of the bugs we reported to the Rust issue tracker. We use them to discuss what Rust does and doesn’t guarantee, why writing correct unsafe Rust is so difficult, and why Rust’s safety model still matters even though its memory safety isn’t perfect.

How we found and validated the bugs

At Microsoft FORGE Lab, we study vulnerabilities in complex software, including the Rust standard library. Our team combines years of experience in vulnerability research with AI-assisted tools that help us investigate code and find bugs that are difficult to uncover through traditional analysis alone.

Some of the bugs in this post were found with help from Hyenas, our research version of codename MDASH. Our researchers investigated the underlying code, reproduced the bugs, assessed their potential security impact, and worked with Rust maintainers to report and fix them.

This post focuses on soundness bugs in the standard library’s unsafe code. Bugs in the compiler itself, such as miscompilations and holes in the type system, are a different topic that we don’t cover here.

Patterns of Rust’s Safety Bugs

At the lowest level, Rust uses unsafe blocks to work with raw pointers and interact directly with the operating system. Much of the standard library, including Vec and String, is built from small unsafe pieces wrapped in safe APIs. Inside an unsafe block, the programmer takes responsibility for the guarantees the compiler can’t check, and that responsibility extends to the safe API built around it. That API must be sound: no matter how safe code uses it, it must be impossible to trigger undefined behavior.

Upholding that promise is harder than it looks. Consider a function that returns the byte at idx from any type that can be viewed as a byte slice, skipping the redundant bounds check after doing its own:

pub fn get<S: AsRef<[u8]>>(s: &S, idx: usize) -> Option<u8> {
    if idx < s.as_ref().len() {
        // SAFETY: we just checked that `idx` is in bounds.
        Some(unsafe { *s.as_ref().get_unchecked(idx) })
    } else {
        None
    }
}

The hard part of unsafe Rust is knowing what you can trust. The function above looks correct, but it assumes that two calls to as_ref return the same slice. Because S is chosen by the caller, a safe AsRef implementation can return a long slice the first time and an empty one the second, and get reads out of bounds. Unsafe code must be careful with every call it makes, and the bugs we found fall into three patterns of misplaced trust: trusting code not to panic, trusting user-provided implementations to be correct, and trusting the underlying system.

Pattern 1: Trusting code not to panic

Unsafe code often breaks an invariant for a moment and restores it afterward; for example, it may allocate an uninitialized buffer and fill it directly, avoiding redundant writes to zero the memory first. That’s fine as long as the function runs to the end. But many operations in Rust can panic, from out-of-bounds indexing to calls into user-provided code, and by default a panic unwinds: it leaves the function early while still running destructors. Unwinding inside that window becomes an invisible exit that exposes the broken invariant to code that trusts it. Bugs of this kind are called panic safety bugs.

MapWindows::clone (#156501)

We identified a panic safety issue in MapWindows::clone. Iterator::map_windows, a nightly API, yields overlapping windows of N items. It keeps the current window in a Buffer whose destructor drops the N items starting at start. In Rust 1.97.0, library/core/src/iter/adapters/map_windows.rs defines it as:

37struct Buffer<T, const N: usize> {
38    // Invariant: `self.buffer[self.start..self.start + N]` is initialized,
39    // with all other elements being uninitialized. This also
40    // implies that `self.start <= N`.
41    buffer: [[MaybeUninit<T>; N]; 2],
42    start: usize,
43}

Buffer::clone, in the same file, built the new buffer first and filled it afterward:

195impl<T: Clone, const N: usize> Clone for Buffer<T, N> {
196    fn clone(&self) -> Self {
197        let mut buffer = Buffer {
198            buffer: [[const { MaybeUninit::uninit() }; N], [const { MaybeUninit::uninit() }; N]],
199            start: self.start,
200        };
201        buffer.as_uninit_array_mut().write(self.as_array_ref().clone());
202        buffer
203    }
204}

After line 197, buffer breaks its own invariant: its slots are uninitialized, but its destructor is already armed. The clone() call on line 201 runs the user’s T::clone before the slots are written. If that call panics, unwinding drops buffer and runs drop_in_place on N uninitialized values. Our proof of concept uses only safe code: an element type whose clone always panics, which causes a crash when the destructor accesses uninitialized memory. The fix holds the new buffer in ManuallyDrop until it is fully written, so unwinding leaks the half-built buffer instead of dropping it.

The general lesson is to treat every call to code you don’t control, such as clone, drop, comparisons, closures, and iterator methods, as a possible early exit. Either finish the work that may panic before breaking an invariant, or make the broken state safe to unwind through: hold it in ManuallyDrop, or use a guard whose destructor restores the invariant, like Vec’s internal SetLenOnDrop. The Rustonomicon covers this under exception safety.

Allocators must not unwind

The recently stabilized Allocator API shows how hard panic safety is to get right. With std, an allocation failure aborts the process by default instead of unwinding, so much of the standard library’s unsafe code assumes allocation never unwinds. Custom allocators can break that assumption. While the API was being stabilized, we reported one place in BTreeMap::insert that becomes unsound when an allocator unwinds, and others reported more (#159334, #159368, #159370). Fixing them one by one would mean auditing everything that allocates, so the stabilization, shipping in Rust 1.100 on November 12, instead requires implementors never to unwind from the trait’s methods or from drop. The proposal notes that “unwinding out of many allocation-related methods was found to be a pervasive source of unsoundness.”

Pattern 2: Trusting user-provided implementations to be correct

Unsafe code often calls into code its caller provides: a comparator, a trait implementation, a closure. That code is safe, but safe doesn’t mean correct, and it can return inconsistent or plainly wrong answers. The question is who is responsible when it does. In C++, it’s the caller. std::sort requires its comparator to be a strict weak ordering, and breaking that rule is undefined behavior. With libstdc++, sorting equal elements with <= reads past the end of the vector:

std::vector<int> v(100, 42);
// Bug: `<=` is not a strict weak ordering, since cmp(a, a) is true.
std::sort(v.begin(), v.end(), [](int a, int b) { return a <= b; });
// AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow in std::__introsort_loop

The same comparator passed to Rust’s sort_by is only a logic error. The sort may panic or leave the slice in an unspecified order, but it never causes undefined behavior. The responsibility sits with the unsafe code. The comparator is safe code supplied by the caller, so the unsafe code inside the sort must stay sound no matter what it returns. The same goes for every safe trait a user can implement: comparisons can be inconsistent, an ExactSizeIterator can report a length that doesn’t match the items it yields, and Borrow can return a different value on each call.

str::replace with a custom Pattern (#156491)

Another of our bug reports shows how easy this trust is to miss: str::replace with a custom Pattern can create a non-UTF-8 String. String search APIs accept any type that implements the nightly Pattern trait, and a pattern can describe itself through as_utf8_pattern. str::replace uses that description to take a fast path when replacing one ASCII byte with another. In Rust 1.96.0, the fast path in library/alloc/src/str.rs looked like this:

268pub fn replace<P: Pattern>(&self, from: P, to: &str) -> String {
269    // Fast path for replacing a single ASCII character with another.
270    if let Some(from_byte) = match from.as_utf8_pattern() {
271        Some(Utf8Pattern::StringPattern([from_byte])) => Some(*from_byte),
272        Some(Utf8Pattern::CharPattern(c)) => c.as_ascii().map(|ascii_char| ascii_char.to_u8()),
273        _ => None,
274    } {
275        if let [to_byte] = to.as_bytes() {
276            return unsafe { replace_ascii(self.as_bytes(), from_byte, *to_byte) };
277        }
278    }

replace_ascii, in the same file, then rewrites the bytes:

708unsafe fn replace_ascii(utf8_bytes: &[u8], from: u8, to: u8) -> String {
709    let result: Vec<u8> = utf8_bytes.iter().map(|b| if *b == from { to } else { *b }).collect();
710    // SAFETY: We replaced ascii with ascii on valid utf8 strings.
711    unsafe { String::from_utf8_unchecked(result) }
712}

The CharPattern branch on line 272 checks that the character is ASCII, but the StringPattern branch on line 271 assumes a one-byte string pattern must be ASCII. That holds for &str patterns, but StringPattern stored &[u8], and as_utf8_pattern is a safe method any Pattern can implement. In our proof of concept, a custom pattern reports the single byte 0x80, which only appears inside multibyte UTF-8 sequences:

impl Pattern for NonAsciiBytePattern {
    // ...
    fn as_utf8_pattern(&self) -> Option<Utf8Pattern<'_>> {
        static NEEDLE: [u8; 1] = [0x80];
        Some(Utf8Pattern::StringPattern(&NEEDLE))
    }
}

// "\u{d000}" is [ed, 80, 80]; the result is [ed, 3f, 3f], which is not UTF-8.
let corrupted = "\u{d000}".replace(NonAsciiBytePattern, "?");

str::replace rewrites the continuation bytes and returns a String that isn’t valid UTF-8, and later string operations that rely on UTF-8 reach undefined behavior. The fix changed StringPattern to hold &str instead of &[u8], so the type itself now guarantees UTF-8.

When unsafe code depends on a property of a user-provided implementation, don’t take it on faith. Call the implementation once and keep the result, validate what it returns, or encode the property in a type that safe code can’t forge, as this fix did. If none of those work, make the trait unsafe so implementors explicitly promise to uphold it.

More examples

join shows how easy it is to fix this kind of bug only partway. In 2020, we reported that it trusted Borrow::borrow to return the same string on each call (CVE-2020-36323), and the fix handled strings that shrink between calls. In April 2026, the same function needed another fix: join borrows the first element twice, and if it grows on the second call, the remaining-length calculation underflows into a heap overflow. The earlier fix had never covered that path.

Others reported similar problems in the Pattern API this year. A safe Pattern can hand back a valid searcher built for a different string, and consumers such as strip_prefix_of apply its ranges to the original string unchecked, reading out of bounds (#158265). The same problem turned up in split_once (#165076) after a report that the Searcher contract doesn’t spell out what str::split relies on (#164904). Both bugs are still open.

Pattern 3: Trusting the underlying system

The first two patterns stay inside Rust code. The third sits at the boundary with the operating system, where unsafe code trusts process-wide state such as signal stacks, memory mappings, and the environment, which other threads, C libraries, or the kernel can touch at any time. These bugs have been hard to find automatically, because a static analyzer would need to model all of that surrounding behavior. AI agents change the picture: they understand enough about the environment the code runs in to make this area practical to search. We started exploring it and found some interesting bugs.

process::exit and the main thread’s signal stack (#161018)

When a thread overflows its stack, Rust prints a clear message and aborts instead of crashing with a bare segmentation fault:

thread 'main' (3307186) has overflowed its stack
fatal runtime error: stack overflow, aborting

This relies on a few pieces of process-wide state. Each thread’s stack ends in a guard page, an inaccessible region just past the stack’s limit: pthread reserves one for every spawned thread, and on Linux the kernel’s own stack guard plays that role for the main thread. Touching it raises SIGSEGV, and Rust registers a handler for that signal. The handler can’t run on the stack that just overflowed, so Rust also gives each thread an alternate signal stack, a small separate mapping with a guard page of its own, which the kernel switches to when it delivers the signal. The handler checks that the faulting address is inside the guard page, prints the message, and aborts.

We found that calling process::exit from a child thread tears down the main thread’s alternate stack while the main thread is still running. process::exit runs the runtime’s cleanup before calling libc’s exit, and in Rust 1.98.0 that cleanup ends in library/std/src/sys/pal/unix/stack_overflow.rs:

196pub unsafe fn cleanup() {
197    if cfg!(panic = "immediate-abort") {
198        return;
199    }
200    // FIXME: I probably cause more bugs than I'm worth!
201    // see https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/111272
202    unsafe { drop_handler(MAIN_ALTSTACK.load(Ordering::Relaxed)) };
203}

Line 202 passes MAIN_ALTSTACK, the main thread’s alternate stack, to drop_handler:

297// SAFETY: we warned the caller this disables the alternate signal stack!
298unsafe { sigaltstack(&disabling_stack, ptr::null_mut()) };
299// SAFETY: We know from `get_stackp` that the alternate stack we installed is part of
300// a mapping that started one page earlier, so walk back a page and unmap from there.
301unsafe { munmap(data.sub(page_size), sigstack_size + page_size) };

Line 298 disables the alternate stack of the calling thread, but line 301 unmaps the main thread’s. The code assumes it runs on the main thread, which isn’t true when a child thread calls process::exit. The main thread keeps running until libc’s exit finishes, with its signal stack registration still pointing at unmapped memory. If it overflows its stack in that window, the kernel can’t deliver the signal, and our proof of concept dies with a plain segmentation fault instead of Rust’s message. The bug dates back to 2015, and the fix stops cleaning up the main thread’s alternate stack altogether.

We also checked whether this could become a security issue. In theory, it could lead to code execution: if a writable mapping landed at the old alternate stack’s address, the kernel would deliver the main thread’s next signal onto it, and another thread could overwrite the handler’s frame, such as its return address, while it runs. In practice, the conditions are very tight. Everything has to happen in the brief window before libc’s exit finishes, the new mapping must have exactly the right size to reuse that address, and overwriting the frame takes a second race inside a short handler. For issue #161018, our testing found no reliable exploitation path under the conditions examined, and we assessed practical exploitation as unlikely. This assessment does not automatically apply to the other issues discussed. The issue has more details in its security impact analysis.

CommandExt::exec and the global environment (#156951)

Our other report involves the process environment. On Unix, CommandExt::exec replaces the current process with a new program. When the command has its own environment variables, exec points the process-global environ at a new array, calls execvp, and restores environ if execvp fails. In Rust 1.99.0, Command::exec takes the environment lock in library/std/src/sys/process/unix/unix.rs:

242let _lock = sys::env::env_read_lock();
243
244let Err(e) = self.do_exec(theirs, envp.as_ref());

Command::do_exec, in the same file, then swaps the environment:

409    _reset = Some(Reset(*sys::env::environ()));
410    *sys::env::environ() = envp.as_ptr();
411}
412
413libc::execvp(self.get_program_cstr().as_ptr(), self.get_argv().as_ptr());
414Err(io::Error::last_os_error())

Line 242 takes only the read side of the environment lock, yet line 410 writes the process-global environ; line 409 saves the old value so it can be restored if execvp on line 413 fails. Writing environ under a read lock lets other threads in. A thread calling env::var takes the same read lock and can see variables meant only for the new program, and two failed exec calls racing each other can leave environ pointing at a freed array that a later env::vars_os() reads. Both proofs of concept use only safe Rust. A 2018 fix held an exclusive lock here, but when the environment lock became a read-write lock in 2021, exec kept the read side. A fix that avoids touching environ by calling execve directly is in review.

The environment has caused trouble before. After a discussion that began in 2015, the 2024 edition marked env::set_var as unsafe, because C functions on most Unix platforms read the environment without going through Rust’s lock.

process::exit and thread-local destructors (#164243)

Getting this boundary right is hard, and more problems are still open. While exploring this area, we independently ran into a double free in safe code that process::exit can cause through thread-local destructors. It was reported by someone else (#164243), but it’s worth mentioning here. libc’s exit first runs the calling thread’s thread-local destructors, as C++ requires, and Rust registers its destructors the same way. If a destructor calls process::exit while a thread local is being replaced, libc drops that thread local a second time. A proposed fix switches process::exit to POSIX _exit, which ends the process without running these handlers.

Conclusion

Every unsafe block rests on assumptions about the code around it. The bugs in this post came from three kinds of misplaced trust:

  • that code won’t panic at the wrong moment,
  • that a caller-provided implementation behaves correctly, and
  • that the process-wide state Rust shares with the operating system and the C library stays the way the code expects.

Familiar patterns are still difficult (Patterns 1 and 2)

The first two patterns are well studied. Rudra looked for both in 2021, and the standard library was already fixing panic safety bugs in 2015 (CVE-2015-20001). They remain challenging to avoid because any call inside unsafe code might unwind or run code the caller supplied.

What we saw this year was mixed. On the positive side, the nightly process is working. Many reports were caught while the affected APIs were still unstable, and several were fixed by changing the design before stabilization. StringPattern now holds &str instead of &[u8], and Allocator was stabilized with a rule that implementors must not unwind. At the same time, bugs in these patterns still reach stable releases, and their fixes aren’t always complete. join was fixed in 2020 and needed another fix in 2026 for a path the first fix had missed.

System boundary bugs are now within reach (Pattern 3)

The third pattern is different. Its bugs live where Rust meets the layers below it: the kernel, through system calls such as sigaltstack and munmap, and the C library, through process-wide state such as environ and the cleanup that libc’s exit runs. Getting them right takes knowledge that lives outside Rust’s type system, which has made these bugs difficult to find with traditional static analysis. That may also be why they last so long. The process::exit signal stack bug was in the standard library for nearly 11 years, and exec has written environ under a read lock since 2021. Unlike our reports in the first two patterns, both affect stable Rust.

Language models already know a great deal about how these interfaces behave, so agentic scanners can check unsafe code against the system it runs on, not just the language. We think this boundary is one of the most promising places for agentic security research, in Rust and beyond.

Rust’s high bar is hard to meet but worth keeping

Rust holds its safe APIs to a stricter standard than C and C++. Safe code must never be able to cause undefined behavior, no matter how it uses an API. In C++, a comparator that breaks std::sort’s ordering requirement causes undefined behavior, while Rust’s sort must stay memory-safe with any Ord implementation. POSIX doesn’t guarantee that setenv is safe to call while another thread reads the environment. That makes memory safety bugs in Rust hard to compare one-to-one with bugs in other languages.

For the same reason, a soundness bug in the standard library isn’t automatically a vulnerability in the programs that use it. Each bug in this post needs an unusual setup to trigger, such as a panic at exactly the wrong moment, a deliberately misbehaving implementation, or calling process::exit from a child thread. It becomes a serious vulnerability only if a real program reaches the API in that way.

Rust’s safety standard is strict and difficult to meet, but it’s also useful. It gives an unambiguous answer to what counts as a soundness bug, so problems can be fixed and prevented once in the library, instead of in every program that uses it. Rust’s safety model strikes the right balance between control, safety, and performance for systems programming, which is why so many projects choose it.

Beyond the lab

At Microsoft FORGE Lab, we’re exploring how technology such as codename MDASH can help researchers find bugs like the ones in this post at greater scale. Rust’s standard library is one of several foundational open source projects where we’re applying this approach.

This research also extends beyond the lab. It helps inform the development of codename MDASH, which brings agentic vulnerability discovery into Microsoft Defender. These findings can also serve as inputs to Microsoft Perception, our new multi-agent security system, where specialized agents work together across broader security workflows. For example, the Web App Pen Test Agent can use codename MDASH findings to help prioritize testing, validate exploitability against live applications, and produce actionable vulnerabilities that downstream agents can use to prioritize and support remediation. This connects AI-powered code analysis with real-world security validation and response, helping security teams move from identifying potential vulnerabilities to understanding and addressing actual risk.

Our goal isn’t to simply find more bugs, it’s to identify meaningful issues, turn those findings into actionable research, and improve the safety of foundational software that developers and organizations depend on.

In C++, it’s the caller. std::sort requires its comparator to be a strict weak ordering, and breaking that rule is undefined behavior. With libstdc++, sorting equal elements with <= reads past the end of the vector:std::vector<int> v(100, 42); // Bug: `<=` is not a strict weak ordering, since cmp(a, a) is true. std::sort(v.begin(), v.end(), [](int a, int b) { return a <= b; }); // AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow in std::__introsort_loop The same comparator passed to Rust’s sort_by is only a logic error. The sort may panic or leave the slice in an unspecified order, but it never causes undefined behavior. The responsibility sits with the unsafe code. The comparator is safe code supplied by the caller, so the unsafe code inside the sort must stay sound no matter what it returns. The same goes for every safe trait a user can implement: comparisons can be inconsistent, an ExactSizeIterator can report a length that doesn’t match the items it yields, and Borrow can return a different value on each call.str::replace with a custom Pattern (#156491)Another of our bug reports shows how easy this trust is to miss: str::replace with a custom Pattern can create a non-UTF-8 String. String search APIs accept any type that implements the nightly Pattern trait, and a pattern can describe itself through as_utf8_pattern. str::replace uses that description to take a fast path when replacing one ASCII byte with another. In Rust 1.96.0, the fast path in library/alloc/src/str.rs looked like this:268pub fn replace<P: Pattern>(&self, from: P, to: &str) -> String { 269 // Fast path for replacing a single ASCII character with another. 270 if let Some(from_byte) = match from.as_utf8_pattern() { 271 Some(Utf8Pattern::StringPattern([from_byte])) => Some(*from_byte), 272 Some(Utf8Pattern::CharPattern(c)) => c.as_ascii().map(|ascii_char| ascii_char.to_u8()), 273 _ => None, 274 } { 275 if let [to_byte] = to.as_bytes() { 276 return unsafe { replace_ascii(self.as_bytes(), from_byte, *to_byte) }; 277 } 278 } replace_ascii, in the same file, then rewrites the bytes:708unsafe fn replace_ascii(utf8_bytes: &[u8], from: u8, to: u8) -> String { 709 let result: Vec<u8> = utf8_bytes.iter().map(|b| if *b == from { to } else { *b }).collect(); 710 // SAFETY: We replaced ascii with ascii on valid utf8 strings. 711 unsafe { String::from_utf8_unchecked(result) } 712} The CharPattern branch on line 272 checks that the character is ASCII, but the StringPattern branch on line 271 assumes a one-byte string pattern must be ASCII. That holds for &str patterns, but StringPattern stored &[u8], and as_utf8_pattern is a safe method any Pattern can implement. In our proof of concept, a custom pattern reports the single byte 0x80, which only appears inside multibyte UTF-8 sequences:impl Pattern for NonAsciiBytePattern { // ... fn as_utf8_pattern(&self) -> Option<Utf8Pattern<'_>> { static NEEDLE: [u8; 1] = [0x80]; Some(Utf8Pattern::StringPattern(&NEEDLE)) } } // "\u{d000}" is [ed, 80, 80]; the result is [ed, 3f, 3f], which is not UTF-8. let corrupted = "\u{d000}".replace(NonAsciiBytePattern, "?"); str::replace rewrites the continuation bytes and returns a String that isn’t valid UTF-8, and later string operations that rely on UTF-8 reach undefined behavior. The fix changed StringPattern to hold &str instead of &[u8], so the type itself now guarantees UTF-8.When unsafe code depends on a property of a user-provided implementation, don’t take it on faith. Call the implementation once and keep the result, validate what it returns, or encode the property in a type that safe code can’t forge, as this fix did. If none of those work, make the trait unsafe so implementors explicitly promise to uphold it.More examplesjoin shows how easy it is to fix this kind of bug only partway. In 2020, we reported that it trusted Borrow::borrow to return the same string on each call (CVE-2020-36323), and the fix handled strings that shrink between calls. In April 2026, the same function needed another fix: join borrows the first element twice, and if it grows on the second call, the remaining-length calculation underflows into a heap overflow. The earlier fix had never covered that path.Others reported similar problems in the Pattern API this year. A safe Pattern can hand back a valid searcher built for a different string, and consumers such as strip_prefix_of apply its ranges to the original string unchecked, reading out of bounds (#158265). The same problem turned up in split_once (#165076) after a report that the Searcher contract doesn’t spell out what str::split relies on (#164904). Both bugs are still open.Pattern 3: Trusting the underlying systemThe first two patterns stay inside Rust code. The third sits at the boundary with the operating system, where unsafe code trusts process-wide state such as signal stacks, memory mappings, and the environment, which other threads, C libraries, or the kernel can touch at any time. These bugs have been hard to find automatically, because a static analyzer would need to model all of that surrounding behavior. AI agents change the picture: they understand enough about the environment the code runs in to make this area practical to search. We started exploring it and found some interesting bugs.process::exit and the main thread’s signal stack (#161018)When a thread overflows its stack, Rust prints a clear message and aborts instead of crashing with a bare segmentation fault:thread 'main' (3307186) has overflowed its stack fatal runtime error: stack overflow, aborting This relies on a few pieces of process-wide state. Each thread’s stack ends in a guard page, an inaccessible region just past the stack’s limit: pthread reserves one for every spawned thread, and on Linux the kernel’s own stack guard plays that role for the main thread. Touching it raises SIGSEGV, and Rust registers a handler for that signal. The handler can’t run on the stack that just overflowed, so Rust also gives each thread an alternate signal stack, a small separate mapping with a guard page of its own, which the kernel switches to when it delivers the signal. The handler checks that the faulting address is inside the guard page, prints the message, and aborts.We found that calling process::exit from a child thread tears down the main thread’s alternate stack while the main thread is still running. process::exit runs the runtime’s cleanup before calling libc’s exit, and in Rust 1.98.0 that cleanup ends in library/std/src/sys/pal/unix/stack_overflow.rs:196pub unsafe fn cleanup() { 197 if cfg!(panic = "immediate-abort") { 198 return; 199 } 200 // FIXME: I probably cause more bugs than I'm worth! 201 // see https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/111272 202 unsafe { drop_handler(MAIN_ALTSTACK.load(Ordering::Relaxed)) }; 203} Line 202 passes MAIN_ALTSTACK, the main thread’s alternate stack, to drop_handler:297// SAFETY: we warned the caller this disables the alternate signal stack! 298unsafe { sigaltstack(&disabling_stack, ptr::null_mut()) }; 299// SAFETY: We know from `get_stackp` that the alternate stack we installed is part of 300// a mapping that started one page earlier, so walk back a page and unmap from there. 301unsafe { munmap(data.sub(page_size), sigstack_size + page_size) }; Line 298 disables the alternate stack of the calling thread, but line 301 unmaps the main thread’s. The code assumes it runs on the main thread, which isn’t true when a child thread calls process::exit. The main thread keeps running until libc’s exit finishes, with its signal stack registration still pointing at unmapped memory. If it overflows its stack in that window, the kernel can’t deliver the signal, and our proof of concept dies with a plain segmentation fault instead of Rust’s message. The bug dates back to 2015, and the fix stops cleaning up the main thread’s alternate stack altogether.We also checked whether this could become a security issue. In theory, it could lead to code execution: if a writable mapping landed at the old alternate stack’s address, the kernel would deliver the main thread’s next signal onto it, and another thread could overwrite the handler’s frame, such as its return address, while it runs. In practice, the conditions are very tight. Everything has to happen in the brief window before libc’s exit finishes, the new mapping must have exactly the right size to reuse that address, and overwriting the frame takes a second race inside a short handler. For issue #161018, our testing found no reliable exploitation path under the conditions examined, and we assessed practical exploitation as unlikely. This assessment does not automatically apply to the other issues discussed. The issue has more details in its security impact analysis.CommandExt::exec and the global environment (#156951)Our other report involves the process environment. On Unix, CommandExt::exec replaces the current process with a new program. When the command has its own environment variables, exec points the process-global environ at a new array, calls execvp, and restores environ if execvp fails. In Rust 1.99.0, Command::exec takes the environment lock in library/std/src/sys/process/unix/unix.rs:242let _lock = sys::env::env_read_lock(); 243 244let Err(e) = self.do_exec(theirs, envp.as_ref()); Command::do_exec, in the same file, then swaps the environment:409 _reset = Some(Reset(*sys::env::environ())); 410 *sys::env::environ() = envp.as_ptr(); 411} 412 413libc::execvp(self.get_program_cstr().as_ptr(), self.get_argv().as_ptr()); 414Err(io::Error::last_os_error()) Line 242 takes only the read side of the environment lock, yet line 410 writes the process-global environ; line 409 saves the old value so it can be restored if execvp on line 413 fails. Writing environ under a read lock lets other threads in. A thread calling env::var takes the same read lock and can see variables meant only for the new program, and two failed exec calls racing each other can leave environ pointing at a freed array that a later env::vars_os() reads. Both proofs of concept use only safe Rust. A 2018 fix held an exclusive lock here, but when the environment lock became a read-write lock in 2021, exec kept the read side. A fix that avoids touching environ by calling execve directly is in review.The environment has caused trouble before. After a discussion that began in 2015, the 2024 edition marked env::set_var as unsafe, because C functions on most Unix platforms read the environment without going through Rust’s lock.process::exit and thread-local destructors (#164243)Getting this boundary right is hard, and more problems are still open. While exploring this area, we independently ran into a double free in safe code that process::exit can cause through thread-local destructors. It was reported by someone else (#164243), but it’s worth mentioning here. libc’s exit first runs the calling thread’s thread-local destructors, as C++ requires, and Rust registers its destructors the same way. If a destructor calls process::exit while a thread local is being replaced, libc drops that thread local a second time. A proposed fix switches process::exit to POSIX _exit, which ends the process without running these handlers.ConclusionEvery unsafe block rests on assumptions about the code around it. The bugs in this post came from three kinds of misplaced trust:that code won’t panic at the wrong moment,that a caller-provided implementation behaves correctly, andthat the process-wide state Rust shares with the operating system and the C library stays the way the code expects.Familiar patterns are still difficult (Patterns 1 and 2)The first two patterns are well studied. Rudra looked for both in 2021, and the standard library was already fixing panic safety bugs in 2015 (CVE-2015-20001). They remain challenging to avoid because any call inside unsafe code might unwind or run code the caller supplied.What we saw this year was mixed. On the positive side, the nightly process is working. Many reports were caught while the affected APIs were still unstable, and several were fixed by changing the design before stabilization. StringPattern now holds &str instead of &[u8], and Allocator was stabilized with a rule that implementors must not unwind. At the same time, bugs in these patterns still reach stable releases, and their fixes aren’t always complete. join was fixed in 2020 and needed another fix in 2026 for a path the first fix had missed.System boundary bugs are now within reach (Pattern 3)The third pattern is different. Its bugs live where Rust meets the layers below it: the kernel, through system calls such as sigaltstack and munmap, and the C library, through process-wide state such as environ and the cleanup that libc’s exit runs. Getting them right takes knowledge that lives outside Rust’s type system, which has made these bugs difficult to find with traditional static analysis. That may also be why they last so long. The process::exit signal stack bug was in the standard library for nearly 11 years, and exec has written environ under a read lock since 2021. Unlike our reports in the first two patterns, both affect stable Rust.Language models already know a great deal about how these interfaces behave, so agentic scanners can check unsafe code against the system it runs on, not just the language. We think this boundary is one of the most promising places for agentic security research, in Rust and beyond.Rust’s high bar is hard to meet but worth keepingRust holds its safe APIs to a stricter standard than C and C++. Safe code must never be able to cause undefined behavior, no matter how it uses an API. In C++, a comparator that breaks std::sort’s ordering requirement causes undefined behavior, while Rust’s sort must stay memory-safe with any Ord implementation. POSIX doesn’t guarantee that setenv is safe to call while another thread reads the environment. That makes memory safety bugs in Rust hard to compare one-to-one with bugs in other languages.For the same reason, a soundness bug in the standard library isn’t automatically a vulnerability in the programs that use it. Each bug in this post needs an unusual setup to trigger, such as a panic at exactly the wrong moment, a deliberately misbehaving implementation, or calling process::exit from a child thread. It becomes a serious vulnerability only if a real program reaches the API in that way.Rust’s safety standard is strict and difficult to meet, but it’s also useful. It gives an unambiguous answer to what counts as a soundness bug, so problems can be fixed and prevented once in the library, instead of in every program that uses it. Rust’s safety model strikes the right balance between control, safety, and performance for systems programming, which is why so many projects choose it.Beyond the labAt Microsoft FORGE Lab, we’re exploring how technology such as codename MDASH can help researchers find bugs like the ones in this post at greater scale. Rust’s standard library is one of several foundational open source projects where we’re applying this approach.This research also extends beyond the lab. It helps inform the development of codename MDASH, which brings agentic vulnerability discovery into Microsoft Defender. These findings can also serve as inputs to Microsoft Perception, our new multi-agent security system, where specialized agents work together across broader security workflows. For example, the Web App Pen Test Agent can use codename MDASH findings to help prioritize testing, validate exploitability against live applications, and produce actionable vulnerabilities that downstream agents can use to prioritize and support remediation. This connects AI-powered code analysis with real-world security validation and response, helping security teams move from identifying potential vulnerabilities to understanding and addressing actual risk.Our goal isn’t to simply find more bugs, it’s to identify meaningful issues, turn those findings into actionable research, and improve the safety of foundational software that developers and organizations depend on.

blocks.html_en: Unsafe code often breaks an invariant for a moment and restores it afterward; for example, it may allocate an uninitialized buffer and fill it directly, avoiding redundant writes to zero the memory first. That’s fine as long as the function runs to the end. But many operations in Rust can panic, from out-of-bounds indexing to calls into user-provided code, and by default a panic unwinds: it leaves the function early while still running destructors. Unwinding inside that window becomes an invisible exit that exposes the broken invariant to code that trusts it. Bugs of this kind are called panic safety bugs.

content_html_zh:
Microsoft’s FORGE Lab found several memory safety issues in Rust’s standard library (std and core), including cases where code written entirely in safe Rust can trigger undefined behavior. The research used Hyenas, FORGE’s frontier research version of codename MDASH, an AI-powered vulnerability-scanning system. The findings reveal three recurring patterns of misplaced trust in unsafe code: trusting code not to panic, trusting user-provided implementations to be correct, and trusting the underlying system.

Rust’s safety guarantees are precisely what make these findings interesting. Its rich type system and ownership model rule out whole classes of memory-safety issues, but much of the standard library relies on unsafe code underneath its safe APIs. When that code breaks its safety contract, even safe Rust can encounter behavior the language is designed to prevent.

Rust’s memory-safety guarantees are increasingly important as the language becomes part of software that billions of people rely on every day. Billions of people are estimated to interact with Rust-based software or operating systems daily, often without knowing it. Microsoft made Rust a Tier-1 internal language alongside C++, C#, and TypeScript, GitHub rewrote the Copilot agent runtime in Rust, and Bun, Android, the Linux kernel, and Cloudflare are moving code to it as well. Much of this software relies on Rust’s foundational libraries, core and std, and the safety guarantees of the APIs they provide. Bugs in those libraries can have consequences well beyond the code where they originate.

Unsafe Rust has been a long-running interest for us. Our team includes the people behind Rudra, a static analyzer that looked for memory-safety bugs across the Rust ecosystem in 2021. We also write many of our own tools in Rust, so its safety is more than a research topic for us. This year, we took a closer look at the standard library to see what kinds of mistakes still show up in its unsafe code today.

In this post, we share some of the bugs we reported to the Rust issue tracker. We use them to discuss what Rust does and doesn’t guarantee, why writing correct unsafe Rust is so difficult, and why Rust’s safety model still matters even though its memory safety isn’t perfect.

How we found and validated the bugs

At Microsoft FORGE Lab, we study vulnerabilities in complex software, including the Rust standard library. Our team combines years of experience in vulnerability research with AI-assisted tools that help us investigate code and find bugs that are difficult to uncover through traditional analysis alone.

Some of the bugs in this post were found with help from Hyenas, our research version of codename MDASH. Our researchers investigated the underlying code, reproduced the bugs, assessed their potential security impact, and worked with Rust maintainers to report and fix them.

This post focuses on soundness bugs in the standard library’s unsafe code. Bugs in the compiler itself, such as miscompilations and holes in the type system, are a different topic that we don’t cover here.

Patterns of Rust’s Safety Bugs

At the lowest level, Rust uses unsafe blocks to work with raw pointers and interact directly with the operating system. Much of the standard library, including Vec and String, is built from small unsafe pieces wrapped in safe APIs. Inside an unsafe block, the programmer takes responsibility for the guarantees the compiler can’t check, and that responsibility extends to the safe API built around it. That API must be sound: no matter how safe code uses it, it must be impossible to trigger undefined behavior.

Upholding that promise is harder than it looks. Consider a function that returns the byte at idx from any type that can be viewed as a byte slice, skipping the redundant bounds check after doing its own:

pub fn get<S: AsRef<[u8]>>(s: &S, idx: usize) -> Option<u8> {
    if idx < s.as_ref().len() {
        // SAFETY: we just checked that `idx` is in bounds.
        Some(unsafe { *s.as_ref().get_unchecked(idx) })
    } else {
        None
    }
}

The hard part of unsafe Rust is knowing what you can trust. The function above looks correct, but it assumes that two calls to as_ref return the same slice. Because S is chosen by the caller, a safe AsRef implementation can return a long slice the first time and an empty one the second, and get reads out of bounds. Unsafe code must be careful with every call it makes, and the bugs we found fall into three patterns of misplaced trust: trusting code not to panic, trusting user-provided implementations to be correct, and trusting the underlying system.

Pattern 1: Trusting code not to panic

Unsafe code often breaks an invariant for a moment and restores it afterward; for example, it may allocate an uninitialized buffer and fill it directly, avoiding redundant writes to zero the memory first. That’s fine as long as the function runs to the end. But many operations in Rust can panic, from out-of-bounds indexing to calls into user-provided code, and by default a panic unwinds: it leaves the function early while still running destructors. Unwinding inside that window becomes an invisible exit that exposes the broken invariant to code that trusts it. Bugs of this kind are called panic safety bugs.

MapWindows::clone (#156501)

We identified a panic safety issue in MapWindows::clone. Iterator::map_windows, a nightly API, yields overlapping windows of N items. It keeps the current window in a Buffer whose destructor drops the N items starting at start. In Rust 1.97.0, library/core/src/iter/adapters/map_windows.rs defines it as:

37struct Buffer<T, const N: usize> {
38    // Invariant: `self.buffer[self.start..self.start + N]` is initialized,
39    // with all other elements being uninitialized. This also
40    // implies that `self.start <= N`.
41    buffer: [[MaybeUninit<T>; N]; 2],
42    start: usize,
43}

Buffer::clone, in the same file, built the new buffer first and filled it afterward:

195impl<T: Clone, const N: usize> Clone for Buffer<T, N> {
196    fn clone(&self) -> Self {
197        let mut buffer = Buffer {
198            buffer: [[const { MaybeUninit::uninit() }; N], [const { MaybeUninit::uninit() }; N]],
199            start: self.start,
200        };
201        buffer.as_uninit_array_mut().write(self.as_array_ref().clone());
202        buffer
203    }
204}

After line 197, buffer breaks its own invariant: its slots are uninitialized, but its destructor is already armed. The clone() call on line 201 runs the user’s T::clone before the slots are written. If that call panics, unwinding drops buffer and runs drop_in_place on N uninitialized values. Our proof of concept uses only safe code: an element type whose clone always panics, which causes a crash when the destructor accesses uninitialized memory. The fix holds the new buffer in ManuallyDrop until it is fully written, so unwinding leaks the half-built buffer instead of dropping it.

The general lesson is to treat every call to code you don’t control, such as clone, drop, comparisons, closures, and iterator methods, as a possible early exit. Either finish the work that may panic before breaking an invariant, or make the broken state safe to unwind through: hold it in ManuallyDrop, or use a guard whose destructor restores the invariant, like Vec’s internal SetLenOnDrop. The Rustonomicon covers this under exception safety.

Allocators must not unwind

The recently stabilized Allocator API shows how hard panic safety is to get right. With std, an allocation failure aborts the process by default instead of unwinding, so much of the standard library’s unsafe code assumes allocation never unwinds. Custom allocators can break that assumption. While the API was being stabilized, we reported one place in BTreeMap::insert that becomes unsound when an allocator unwinds, and others reported more (#159334, #159368, #159370). Fixing them one by one would mean auditing everything that allocates, so the stabilization, shipping in Rust 1.100 on November 12, instead requires implementors never to unwind from the trait’s methods or from drop. The proposal notes that “unwinding out of many allocation-related methods was found to be a pervasive source of unsoundness.”

Pattern 2: Trusting user-provided implementations to be correct

Unsafe code often calls into code its caller provides: a comparator, a trait implementation, a closure. That code is safe, but safe doesn’t mean correct, and it can return inconsistent or plainly wrong answers. The question is who is responsible when it does. In C++, it’s the caller. std::sort requires its comparator to be a strict weak ordering, and breaking that rule is undefined behavior. With libstdc++, sorting equal elements with <= reads past the end of the vector:

std::vector<int> v(100, 42);
// Bug: `<=` is not a strict weak ordering, since cmp(a, a) is true.
std::sort(v.begin(), v.end(), [](int a, int b) { return a <= b; });
// AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow in std::__introsort_loop

The same comparator passed to Rust’s sort_by is only a logic error. The sort may panic or leave the slice in an unspecified order, but it never causes undefined behavior. The responsibility sits with the unsafe code. The comparator is safe code supplied by the caller, so the unsafe code inside the sort must stay sound no matter what it returns. The same goes for every safe trait a user can implement: comparisons can be inconsistent, an ExactSizeIterator can report a length that doesn’t match the items it yields, and Borrow can return a different value on each call.

str::replace with a custom Pattern (#156491)

Another of our bug reports shows how easy this trust is to miss: str::replace with a custom Pattern can create a non-UTF-8 String. String search APIs accept any type that implements the nightly Pattern trait, and a pattern can describe itself through as_utf8_pattern. str::replace uses that description to take a fast path when replacing one ASCII byte with another. In Rust 1.96.0, the fast path in library/alloc/src/str.rs looked like this:

268pub fn replace<P: Pattern>(&self, from: P, to: &str) -> String {
269    // Fast path for replacing a single ASCII character with another.
270    if let Some(from_byte) = match from.as_utf8_pattern() {
271        Some(Utf8Pattern::StringPattern([from_byte])) => Some(*from_byte),
272        Some(Utf8Pattern::CharPattern(c)) => c.as_ascii().map(|ascii_char| ascii_char.to_u8()),
273        _ => None,
274    } {
275        if let [to_byte] = to.as_bytes() {
276            return unsafe { replace_ascii(self.as_bytes(), from_byte, *to_byte) };
277        }
278    }

replace_ascii, in the same file, then rewrites the bytes:

708unsafe fn replace_ascii(utf8_bytes: &[u8], from: u8, to: u8) -> String {
709    let result: Vec<u8> = utf8_bytes.iter().map(|b| if *b == from { to } else { *b }).collect();
710    // SAFETY: We replaced ascii with ascii on valid utf8 strings.
711    unsafe { String::from_utf8_unchecked(result) }
712}

The CharPattern branch on line 272 checks that the character is ASCII, but the StringPattern branch on line 271 assumes a one-byte string pattern must be ASCII. That holds for &str patterns, but StringPattern stored &[u8], and as_utf8_pattern is a safe method any Pattern can implement. In our proof of concept, a custom pattern reports the single byte 0x80, which only appears inside multibyte UTF-8 sequences:

impl Pattern for NonAsciiBytePattern {
    // ...
    fn as_utf8_pattern(&self) -> Option<Utf8Pattern<'_>> {
        static NEEDLE: [u8; 1] = [0x80];
        Some(Utf8Pattern::StringPattern(&NEEDLE))
    }
}

// "\u{d000}" is [ed, 80, 80]; the result is [ed, 3f, 3f], which is not UTF-8.
let corrupted = "\u{d000}".replace(NonAsciiBytePattern, "?");

str::replace rewrites the continuation bytes and returns a String that isn’t valid UTF-8, and later string operations that rely on UTF-8 reach undefined behavior. The fix changed StringPattern to hold &str instead of &[u8], so the type itself now guarantees UTF-8.

When unsafe code depends on a property of a user-provided implementation, don’t take it on faith. Call the implementation once and keep the result, validate what it returns, or encode the property in a type that safe code can’t forge, as this fix did. If none of those work, make the trait unsafe so implementors explicitly promise to uphold it.

join shows how easy it is to fix this kind of bug only partway. In 2020, we reported that it trusted Borrow::borrow to return the same string on each call (CVE-2020-36323), and the fix handled strings that shrink between calls. In April 2026, the same function needed another fix: join borrows the first element twice, and if it grows on the second call, the remaining-length calculation underflows into a heap overflow. The earlier fix had never covered that path.

Others reported similar problems in the Pattern API this year. A safe Pattern can hand back a valid searcher built for a different string, and consumers such as strip_prefix_of apply its ranges to the original string unchecked, reading out of bounds (#158265). The same problem turned up in split_once (#165076) after a report that the Searcher contract doesn’t spell out what str::split relies on (#164904). Both bugs are still open.

Pattern 3: Trusting the underlying system

The first two patterns stay inside Rust code. The third sits at the boundary with the operating system, where unsafe code trusts process-wide state such as signal stacks, memory mappings, and the environment, which other threads, C libraries, or the kernel can touch at any time. These bugs have been hard to find automatically, because a static analyzer would need to model all of that surrounding behavior. AI agents change the picture: they understand enough about the environment the code runs in to make this area practical to search. We started exploring it and found some interesting bugs.

process::exit and the main thread’s signal stack (#161018)

When a thread overflows its stack, Rust prints a clear message and aborts instead of crashing with a bare segmentation fault:

thread 'main' (3307186) has overflowed its stack
fatal runtime error: stack overflow, aborting

This relies on a few pieces of process-wide state. Each thread’s stack ends in a guard page, an inaccessible region just past the stack’s limit: pthread reserves one for every spawned thread, and on Linux the kernel’s own stack guard plays that role for the main thread. Touching it raises SIGSEGV, and Rust registers a handler for that signal. The handler can’t run on the stack that just overflowed, so Rust also gives each thread an alternate signal stack, a small separate mapping with a guard page of its own, which the kernel switches to when it delivers the signal. The handler checks that the faulting address is inside the guard page, prints the message, and aborts.

We found that calling process::exit from a child thread tears down the main thread’s alternate stack while the main thread is still running. process::exit runs the runtime’s cleanup before calling libc’s exit, and in Rust 1.98.0 that cleanup ends in library/std/src/sys/pal/unix/stack_overflow.rs:

196pub unsafe fn cleanup() {
197    if cfg!(panic = "immediate-abort") {
198        return;
199    }
200    // FIXME: I probably cause more bugs than I'm worth!
201    // see https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/111272
202    unsafe { drop_handler(MAIN_ALTSTACK.load(Ordering::Relaxed)) };
203}

Line 202 passes MAIN_ALTSTACK, the main thread’s alternate stack, to drop_handler:

297// SAFETY: we warned the caller this disables the alternate signal stack!
298unsafe { sigaltstack(&disabling_stack, ptr::null_mut()) };
299// SAFETY: We know from `get_stackp` that the alternate stack we installed is part of
300// a mapping that started one page earlier, so walk back a page and unmap from there.
301unsafe { munmap(data.sub(page_size), sigstack_size + page_size) };

Line 298 disables the alternate stack of the calling thread, but line 301 unmaps the main thread’s. The code assumes it runs on the main thread, which isn’t true when a child thread calls process::exit. The main thread keeps running until libc’s exit finishes, with its signal stack registration still pointing at unmapped memory. If it overflows its stack in that window, the kernel can’t deliver the signal, and our proof of concept dies with a plain segmentation fault instead of Rust’s message. The bug dates back to 2015, and the fix stops cleaning up the main thread’s alternate stack altogether.

We also checked whether this could become a security issue. In theory, it could lead to code execution: if a writable mapping landed at the old alternate stack’s address, the kernel would deliver the main thread’s next signal onto it, and another thread could overwrite the handler’s frame, such as its return address, while it runs. In practice, the conditions are very tight. Everything has to happen in the brief window before libc’s exit finishes, the new mapping must have exactly the right size to reuse that address, and overwriting the frame takes a second race inside a short handler. For issue #161018, our testing found no reliable exploitation path under the conditions examined, and we assessed practical exploitation as unlikely. This assessment does not automatically apply to the other issues discussed. The issue has more details in its security impact analysis.

CommandExt::exec and the global environment (#156951)

Our other report involves the process environment. On Unix, CommandExt::exec replaces the current process with a new program. When the command has its own environment variables, exec points the process-global environ at a new array, calls execvp, and restores environ if execvp fails. In Rust 1.99.0, Command::exec takes the environment lock in library/std/src/sys/process/unix/unix.rs:

242let _lock = sys::env::env_read_lock();
243
244let Err(e) = self.do_exec(theirs, envp.as_ref());

Command::do_exec, in the same file, then swaps the environment:

409    _reset = Some(Reset(*sys::env::environ()));
410    *sys::env::environ() = envp.as_ptr();
411}
412

Line 242 takes only the read side of the environment lock, yet line 410 writes the process-global environ; line 409 saves the old value so it can be restored if execvp on line 413 fails. Writing environ under a read lock lets other threads in. A thread calling env::var takes the same read lock and can see variables meant only for the new program, and two failed exec calls racing each other can leave environ pointing at a freed array that a later env::vars_os() reads. Both proofs of concept use only safe Rust. A 2018 fix held an exclusive lock here, but when the environment lock became a read-write lock in 2021, exec kept the read side. A fix that avoids touching environ by calling execve directly is in review.

The environment has caused trouble before. After a discussion that began in 2015, the 2024 edition marked env::set_var as unsafe, because C functions on most Unix platforms read the environment without going through Rust’s lock.

process::exit and thread-local destructors (#164243)

Getting this boundary right is hard, and more problems are still open. While exploring this area, we independently ran into a double free in safe code that process::exit can cause through thread-local destructors. It was reported by someone else (#164243), but it’s worth mentioning here. libc’s exit first runs the calling thread’s thread-local destructors, as C++ requires, and Rust registers its destructors the same way. If a destructor calls process::exit while a thread local is being replaced, libc drops that thread local a second time. A proposed fix switches process::exit to POSIX _exit, which ends the process without running these handlers.

结论

Every unsafe block rests on assumptions about the code around it. The bugs in this post came from three kinds of misplaced trust:

  • that code won’t panic at the wrong moment,
  • that a caller-provided implementation behaves correctly, and
  • that the process-wide state Rust shares with the operating system and the C library stays the way the code expects.

Familiar patterns are still difficult (Patterns 1 and 2)

The first two patterns are well studied. Rudra looked for both in 2021, and the standard library was already fixing panic safety bugs in 2015 (CVE-2015-20001). They remain challenging to avoid because any call inside unsafe code might unwind or run code the caller supplied.

What we saw this year was mixed. On the positive side, the nightly process is working. Many reports were caught while the affected APIs were still unstable, and several were fixed by changing the design before stabilization. StringPattern now holds &str instead of &[u8], and Allocator was stabilized with a rule that implementors must not unwind. At the same time, bugs in these patterns still reach stable releases, and their fixes aren’t always complete. join was fixed in 2020 and needed another fix in 2026 for a path the first fix had missed.

System boundary bugs are now within reach (Pattern 3)

The third pattern is different. Its bugs live where Rust meets the layers below it: the kernel, through system calls such as sigaltstack and munmap, and the C library, through process-wide state such as environ and the cleanup that libc’s exit runs. Getting them right takes knowledge that lives outside Rust’s type system, which has made these bugs difficult to find with traditional static analysis. That may also be why they last so long. The process::exit signal stack bug was in the standard library for nearly 11 years, and exec has written environ under a read lock since 2021. Unlike our reports in the first two patterns, both affect stable Rust.

Language models already know a great deal about how these interfaces behave, so agentic scanners can check unsafe code against the system it runs on, not just the language. We think this boundary is one of the most promising places for agentic security research, in Rust and beyond.

Rust’s high bar is hard to meet but worth keeping

Rust holds its safe APIs to a stricter standard than C and C++. Safe code must never be able to cause undefined behavior, no matter how it uses an API. In C++, a comparator that breaks std::sort’s ordering requirement causes undefined behavior, while Rust’s sort must stay memory-safe with any Ord implementation. POSIX doesn’t guarantee that setenv is safe to call while another thread reads the environment. That makes memory safety bugs in Rust hard to compare one-to-one with bugs in other languages.

For the same reason, a soundness bug in the standard library isn’t automatically a vulnerability in the programs that use it. Each bug in this post needs an unusual setup to trigger, such as a panic at exactly the wrong moment, a deliberately misbehaving implementation, or calling process::exit from a child thread. It becomes a serious vulnerability only if a real program reaches the API in that way.

Rust’s safety standard is strict and difficult to meet, but it’s also useful. It gives an unambiguous answer to what counts as a soundness bug, so problems can be fixed and prevented once in the library, instead of in every program that uses it. Rust’s safety model strikes the right balance between control, safety, and performance for systems programming, which is why so many projects choose it.

Beyond the lab

At Microsoft FORGE Lab, we’re exploring how technology such as codename MDASH can help researchers find bugs like the ones in this post at greater scale. Rust’s standard library is one of several foundational open source projects where we’re applying this approach.

This research also extends beyond the lab. It helps inform the development of codename MDASH, which brings agentic vulnerability discovery into Microsoft Defender. These findings can also serve as inputs to Microsoft Perception, our new multi-agent security system, where specialized agents work together across broader security workflows. For example, the Web App Pen Test Agent can use codename MDASH findings to help prioritize testing, validate exploitability against live applications, and produce actionable vulnerabilities that downstream agents can use to prioritize and support remediation. This connects AI-powered code analysis with real-world security validation and response, helping security teams move from identifying potential vulnerabilities to understanding and addressing actual risk.

Our goal isn’t to simply find more bugs, it’s to identify meaningful issues, turn those findings into actionable research, and improve the safety of foundational software that developers and organizations depend on.
